claims.text: Introducing additional chemically disparate elements into a multicomponent transition-metal catalyst increases local lattice distortion.
Increased local lattice distortion shifts the d-band center of surface active sites.
The d-band-center shift enhances adsorption and activation of reaction intermediates.
Enhanced adsorption and activation of intermediates improves catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
The intended initial material is a nanostructured, phase-stable binary or ternary transition-metal catalyst with a well-defined active surface and relatively low lattice distortion.
Additional transition metals can be incorporated while retaining the overall crystalline structure.
Local surface lattice distortion can be quantified through changes in interatomic distances and broadening of local coordination environments.
A distortion-induced d-band-center shift tunes the binding energies of reactive intermediates.
Tuned intermediate binding produces more favorable adsorption-desorption kinetics.
More favorable adsorption-desorption kinetics increase catalytic turnover and selectivity.
Increased lattice distortion stabilizes the catalyst against structural degradation over time.
Relative to the simpler-composition baseline, the more distorted multicomponent catalyst will have a higher turnover frequency.
Relative to the baseline, the more distorted multicomponent catalyst will have greater selectivity for the desired reaction.
Relative to the baseline, the more distorted multicomponent catalyst will retain structural integrity for longer during reaction.
The modified catalyst will exhibit a measurable d-band-center shift consistent with enhanced adsorption.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to nanostructured transition-metal catalysts that remain phase-stable under moderate- to high-temperature catalytic conditions.
The hypothesis may not apply when substantial phase transformations occur or when a support material predominantly governs activity.
The relative roles of electronic modification and strain-induced effects, and the optimal lattice-distortion range, remain uncertain.
EXAFS and XRD can characterize local structure, while XPS and UPS can quantify d-band-center positions in the proposed comparison.
Failure to observe a statistically significant performance improvement or a corresponding d-band-center shift would falsify the hypothesis.
